facts.statement: The species was originally classified under the genus Xenacanthus as Xenacanthus luedersensis before being moved to its own genus.
This extinct genus lived during the Early Permian and possibly the upper Pennsylvanian periods in North America.
facts.quote: Barbclabornia is an extinct genus of xenacanth from the Early Permian and possibly upper Pennsylvanian of North America.

facts.statement: Fossils have been discovered in the Clear Fork, Albany, Wichita, and Dunkard Groups within the Asselian and Atinskian formations.
facts.quote: It has been found in several places within Asselian and Atinskian formations, including the Clear Fork, Albany, Wichita, and Dunkard Groups.

facts.statement: The animal was first identified in 1970 solely from isolated teeth that were mistakenly assigned to the genus Xenacanthus.
facts.quote: Barbclabornia was initially only known from isolated teeth, which were assigned to the genus Xenacanthus in 1970 based on the belief that all Upper Paleozoic xenacanthids belonged to said genus.

facts.statement: In 2003, the species was moved to a new genus following the description of unique tooth structures and the discovery of a large jawbone at Lake Frederick.
facts.quote: In 2003, X. luedersensis would be reassigned to a new genus after differences in tooth structure were described, and with the discovery of a large palatoquadrate bearing luedersensis teeth at Lake Frederick.

facts.statement: The genus name honors Barbara and Alvie Claborn, who discovered and prepared the key jaw fossil.
facts.quote: The genus Barbclabornia honors Barbara and Alvie Claborn, who discovered and helped prepare the palatoquadrate respectively.

facts.statement: The teeth resemble those of the genus Bransonella, suggesting a close evolutionary relationship between the two.
facts.quote: The teeth of Barbclabornia are similar to those of Bransonella, and as such are believed to be related.

facts.statement: The teeth are extremely small, measuring only 1 to 3 millimeters in height.
facts.quote: They are very small, being between 1–3 mm tall.

facts.statement: Tiny, claw-like denticles found on the animal are believed to have originated from a fold in the mucous membrane.
facts.quote: These denticles are assumed to be from the mucous membrane fold.

facts.statement: The known jawbone fragment is 37.5 cm long, though scientists estimate the complete jaw would have reached 45 cm.
facts.quote: The palatoquadrate is 37.5 cm (14.7 in) long and incomplete, but is assumed to have a total length of 45 cm (17.7 in).

facts.statement: Based on jaw size comparisons, this species is estimated to be the largest xenacanthid ever discovered.
facts.quote: This would make it the largest xenacanthid ever found.

facts.statement: Chemical analysis of the fossils confirms that this animal lived exclusively in freshwater environments.
facts.quote: Combined δ18OP and 87Sr/86Sr measurements confirm that Barbclabornia was a freshwater inhabitant.

facts.statement: Researchers later proposed that the animal was a filter feeder similar to modern basking sharks and whale sharks, consuming zooplankton.
facts.quote: However, Johnson alongside Jiri Zidek, William May, and Alvie Claborn would instead compare the large xenacanth with numerous tiny teeth to be analogous to modern filter feeding sharks, the Basking Shark and Whale Shark.

facts.statement: There is a scientific debate regarding its diet, with initial theories suggesting it swallowed prey whole, while later research suggests it was a filter feeder.
facts.quote: Paleontologist Gary D. Johnson initially proposed that the shark could only bite down on its prey and swallow it whole. This would give it a diet of less active prey, primarily small fish, amphibians, and arthropods.

facts.statement: The genus belongs to the parent group Bransonelliformes.
This animal is classified within the class Chondrichthyes, which includes sharks and rays.
The species lived between 303.7 and 274.4 million years ago, spanning the Gzhelian to Kungurian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Gzhelian to Kungurian (303.7 to 274.4 million years ago)
